title: Fate Marable records for OKeh and the band personnel
summary: Mason recalls making OKeh records on alto with Fate Marable's orchestra and lists the members; he regrets the band stayed on the boat.

A fellow by Sidney, oh, I can't think of his last name on the trumpet. He had two trumpets. He's a New Orleans trumpet player. Desveen? Sidney Desveen. Yeah, Sidney Desveen playing trumpets. And we had Walter Thomas playing third alto, Bert Bailey playing tennis saxophone, and I played myself, Norman, played alto.
Is Walter Thomas the one that was known as Foots? Well, no. It is a different Walter Thomas.

Well, as a matter of fact, he left our band and went to Cab Calloway's band, but he died shortly after something, for some reason, he did. I think he had cancer, and he died shortly after he went with Cab's band. And, let's see. Yeah, we had a fellow by the name of Foster. George Foster's brother was playing the banjo. He played a banjo, and the bass player was Henry Kimball. Henry, old man Kimball. Henry Kimball was the bass player. That was the group that made that record.
That must have been about, what, 27? Just about. Around 27, yes. Yes. Yes.

Yes. Well, it was, that band, it was rather unfortunate that the fellows didn't want to go no place but on the boat, because I was quite sure the band would have been very well, would have been very properly known, of course, and probably we would have made other records. However, at that time there was not so much emphasis on records as it is now. You see, recording now is quite an important part of a band's getting a band popular and also making money. At that time, it cost, I guess, the facilities then for broadcasting wasn't quite up to where they are now, and there was not quite as much demand for records as they are now in that you didn't have all these stereophonics and hi-fis and all that kind of stuff. As a matter of fact, the industry was not putting out quite as much money to attract the buying public as they are now, and I guess that's one of the reasons why we didn't concentrate anymore on making records.
